Series::has_sensitivity¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::has_sensitivity() const -> bool

What It Does¶

has_sensitivity() tells you whether this Series currently stores a reverse-mode sensitivity value.

That wording is deliberate.

The method answers a storage-state question, not a mathematical question. It does not ask whether the correct derivative would be zero or nonzero. It asks whether a reverse pass has populated a stored sensitivity on this value and that stored value has not since been cleared.

This makes has_sensitivity() the right companion to sensitivity(), especially because the current public surface returns a zero-valued series from sensitivity() even before any reverse pass has populated one.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true if a stored sensitivity currently exists on this Series, otherwise false.

Relationship To Nearby Methods¶

  • tracks_slope() answers “is this series configured to receive reverse-mode sensitivity if propagation reaches it?”

  • has_sensitivity() answers “does this series currently hold a stored reverse-mode result?”

  • sensitivity() reads that stored result itself

Those are related, but they are different stages:

  1. configure tracking

  2. run reverse-mode

  3. inspect whether a stored result exists

  4. read the stored result

Mathematical Meaning¶

Suppose a tracked leaf x participates in a scalar objective L.

After reverse() runs, the stored value on x is the sensitivity dL/dx.

has_sensitivity() does not tell you what dL/dx is. It only tells you whether that quantity is currently stored on the object.

That distinction matters because a stored sensitivity can legitimately be all zeros, and on the current public surface a not-yet-populated sensitivity also reads back as zeros through sensitivity().

Examples¶

Example 1. A tracked Series starts without stored sensitivity, gains it after reverse, and loses it again after clearing.

auto life = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 8.0}, pluss::cfg::tracks_slope());

std::cout << "before=" << (life.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
life.log().sum().reverse();
std::cout << "after_reverse=" << (life.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
life.clear();
std::cout << "after_clear=" << (life.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";

The scalar objective is

L = log(2) + log(4) + log(8)

so a real reverse pass does occur and produces a real stored sensitivity. has_sensitivity() is the boolean check that this stored result exists.

Output¶

before=false
after_reverse=true
after_clear=false

Example 2. has_sensitivity() is only ever true after a reverse pass over a tracked leaf. Reverse-mode over an objective with no tracked leaf does not fall through to an empty result — it raises.

auto silent_x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});

try {
  silent_x.mul(2.0).sum().reverse();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

std::cout << "has_dL_dx=" << (silent_x.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";

The scalar objective L = 2x₁ + 2x₂ + 2x₃ is mathematically differentiable, but silent_x was never configured as a tracked leaf, so the graph is disconnected and reverse() reports it. has_sensitivity() is still false afterward — nothing was stored.

Output¶

series_tape::backpropagate: objective does not track slope and has no source link; nothing to differentiate (a constant, or built only from non-differentiable ops)
has_dL_dx=false

Example 3. has_sensitivity() is the way to distinguish “no stored sensitivity yet” from “a stored sensitivity that happens to contain zeros.”

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

std::cout << "has_dL_dx=" << (x.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
std::cout << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

has_dL_dx=false
pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

The zero values alone do not prove a reverse pass happened. The boolean state from has_sensitivity() is what disambiguates that case.

Example 4. A retained intermediate can also report stored sensitivity after reverse.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto mid = x.mul(2.0);
mid.retain_grad();
mid.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "mid_has_dL_dmid=" << (mid.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
std::cout << "x_has_dL_dx=" << (x.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";

Here mid = 2x, and the scalar objective is

L = sum(mid)

so dL/dmid = [1, 1, 1] and dL/dx = [2, 2, 2]. Because mid was marked to retain its own sensitivity, both booleans become true.

Output¶

mid_has_dL_dmid=true
x_has_dL_dx=true

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • has_sensitivity() can be false even when tracks_slope() is true.

  • A zero-valued sensitivity() result does not imply has_sensitivity() is true.

  • Clearing sensitivity resets this method back to false without disabling tracking.

  • On intermediates, this method is usually only interesting when retention was enabled first.

Summary¶

Use has_sensitivity() as the authoritative test for whether a Series currently stores reverse-mode sensitivity. It answers a storage-state question, not a derivative-value question.

See Also¶

  • Series::sensitivity: read the stored value itself.

  • Series::tracks_slope: inspect tracking configuration.

  • Series::clear: clear stored sensitivity.
